source_text: Advertis ergo quantam distinctionem superficies verborum fecerit de naturis duarum plebium: Israelitas filios Dei vocat, et Chananaeos semen maledictum. Si hoc quod sonat ad generationes referretur et partus; dicendum erat, aliam esse religiosorum generationem, aliam profanorum.
pass_a_gloss: You notice therefore how great a distinction the surface of the words made about the natures of two peoples: he calls the Israelites sons of God, and the Canaanites a cursed seed. If this which sounds were referred to generations and births; it would have to be said that there is one generation of the religious, another of the profane.

lemmas.lexica: LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS malum; Blaise malum naturale vs malum voluntatis

pass_b_english: You see, then, what a distinction the surface of the words makes between the natures of the two peoples: it calls the Israelites God’s children and the Canaanites a cursed seed. If the sound of these words referred to generation and birth, one would have to say that the generation of the devout differed from that of the profane.

choices.why: Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.
Seed is God's work in generation; Julian refuses to make semen a vehicle of natural evil.
rejected: original sin (later system as default gloss)
traducianism of the soul (not the load here)

choices.why: Julian's Manichaean charge: an evil that is a nature, not a will's act.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
